title: Language and Radiators
premise: Rafael Kavanagh, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after his mother's death, has spent nine years writing reviews he cannot verify and letters he never sends. When renovating the family flat, he finds a box of undelivered letters behind the wardrobe—his own, and his mother's to him—revealing she knew he was drifting away and begged him, in drafts she never posted, to come home. As the last bus route to the old neighborhood is scheduled for permanent rerouting, Rafael must trace the people those letters were meant for: a estranged brother, a first love, a retired chef whose cooking once made him feel real. In saying each goodbye aloud, he discovers taste returning—not as nostalgia but as permission to belong somewhere new. The book ends on the final run of the 47 bus, Rafael speaking his mother's last letter out loud to a car of strangers, tasting salt and sweetness at once.
about_author: Tamsin Halloran is a former line cook turned essayist who writes about food, memory, and the families we fail in small daily ways. She lives above a closed-down chippy and insists this is research.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He files his latest review—a rave for a meal he tasted nothing of—and catalogs the unsaid things in his life like pantry stock. Emotional beat: polished numbness cracking slightly when a young waiter asks if the food was 'really that good.'

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Clearing his late mother's flat for sale, he pries loose a panel and finds a shoebox: forty undelivered letters, half hers, half his own returned unopened. Emotional beat: vertigo—the past refusing to stay filed.

chapters.title: What She Wrote First
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, interleaved with his mother Nuala's letter-voice. Her earliest letter asks why he stopped calling; her handwriting gets shakier across the years. Emotional beat: guilt arriving not as accusation but as patience.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Kept the House
chapters.summary: Rafael visits Declan, who stayed in the old neighborhood running the family's fading pub. Declan knew about the letters and chose silence to protect him. Emotional beat: loyalty revealed as its own kind of lie.

chapters.title: Route 47
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He learns the bus line to the old neighborhood is being rerouted permanently in six weeks—an arbitrary deadline that suddenly structures everything. Emotional beat: panic disguised as logistics.

chapters.title: A Reviewer Who Cannot Taste
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. His editor, suspicious of his recent superlatives, offers him a profile piece on Chef Ivo Marchetti—the man who trained his palate decades ago. Emotional beat: dread and hunger braided together.

chapters.title: The Kitchen Where I Was Real
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Rafael's POV. Seventeen-year-old Rafael washing pots in Marchetti's kitchen, learning that flavor is attention. Emotional beat: warmth remembered so vividly it hurts.

chapters.title: Letters to Sorcha
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Three unsent letters are addressed to Sorcha Byrne, his first love, now a hospice nurse two towns over. He drafts a call script and deletes it four times. Emotional beat: cowardice examined without excuse.

chapters.title: Declan's Version
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. At the pub, Declan remembers their mother differently—sterner, funnier, less saintly—and resents Rafael's grief-gloss. Emotional beat: truth as friction between siblings.

chapters.title: The Palate Test
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He eats alone at a mediocre diner and realizes he can't distinguish the dishes at all; he has been fabricating reviews from technique alone. Emotional beat: professional identity collapsing quietly.

chapters.title: Sorcha Answers
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. She calls him first, having heard through Declan. Their conversation is awkward, funny, and devastatingly ordinary. Emotional beat: the relief of being known badly and still welcomed.

chapters.title: Marchetti's Hands
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He visits the aging chef, who is losing his own senses to illness and recognizes Rafael's condition instantly. Emotional beat: mentorship inverted—the student confessing, the teacher forgiving.

chapters.title: The Letter That Was Never Finished
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The box's final letter, in Nuala's hand, breaks off mid-sentence the week before she died. He becomes obsessed with completing it. Emotional beat: obsession as avoidance of grief.

chapters.title: What Declan Never Sent
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Declan admits he found one of Nuala's letters years ago and hid it because it asked Rafael to come home and Declan couldn't bear competing. Emotional beat: betrayal and tenderness in the same breath.

chapters.title: Rupture
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A fight at the pub over the hidden letter turns vicious; old wounds about who was 'the loyal one' surface. Rafael walks into the rain. Emotional beat: the cost of every kept secret arriving at once.

chapters.title: Sorcha's Shift
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. She shows Rafael her hospice ward, where patients say last things nightly, and challenges him: goodbyes aren't for the dying, they're for the living. Emotional beat: quiet, hard clarity.

chapters.title: Taste
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Cooking Nuala's soda bread recipe in her kitchen, he tastes something—faint, unmistakable, hers. Emotional beat: grief and flavor arriving together, unwilled.

chapters.title: Confessions in Print
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He writes the profile of Marchetti as a confession—admitting he cannot taste, and what that taught him about honesty. His editor holds it, furious and moved. Emotional beat: choosing truth over reputation.

chapters.title: The Last Week of the 47
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided—Rafael, Declan, Sorcha—as the reroute date nears and each prepares for the final ride in their own way. Emotional beat: converging timelines, held breath.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Climax. Rafael boards the final 47 with Declan and Sorcha, stands, and reads Nuala's unfinished letter aloud, finishing it in his own words before a busload of strangers. Emotional beat: exposure transformed into belonging.

chapters.title: Aftertaste
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The review publishes; readers write in with their own inventories of unsaid things. He and Declan repaint the pub's back room where the wardrobe stood. Emotional beat: forgiveness as ongoing practice.

chapters.title: The New Route
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, closing. He takes a job reviewing honestly or not at all, cooks Sunday dinners at the pub, and mails one last letter—to himself, then burns it. Emotional beat: home redefined as something you say yes to, repeatedly, out loud.
